records.geometric_relation: The standard Watson-Crick G-C base pair forms three hydrogen bonds: guanine N1 to cytosine N3, guanine N2 to cytosine O2, and guanine O6 to cytosine N4. All three donor/acceptor distances are direct measurements on the deposited coordinates for this specific base pair.

conditions: First model, ATOM records only; ideal Watson-Crick atom naming per the deposited residue (N1/N2/O6 for guanine, N3/O2/N4 for cytosine).

limitations: Static deposited crystal model; not a claim about hydrogen-bond dynamics, base-pair breathing, or solution behavior.
One specific base pair in a 12-bp duplex; not a survey of hydrogen-bond geometry across the whole sequence.

items.question: The supplied atoms form the three Watson-Crick hydrogen bonds of a real G-C base pair (guanine, chain A residue 2; cytosine, chain B residue 23) in a B-DNA dodecamer. Calculate all three donor-acceptor distances: N1(G)-N3(C), N2(G)-O2(C), and O6(G)-N4(C). Report each distance in angstrom to three decimal places. A Watson-Crick A-T pair instead forms only two hydrogen bonds (N1-N3 and N6-O4). Which base pair type would you expect to be more thermally stable, and why?

Coordinates are in angstrom (1 nm = 10 angstrom). XYZ atom rows are one-based after the two header lines. items.rubric: 8 points: three distances (6; 0.01 angstrom each), correct identification that G-C pairs (3 hydrogen bonds) are expected to be more thermally stable than A-T pairs (2 hydrogen bonds), with the reasoning that more hydrogen bonds per base pair means more energy is required to separate the strands at that position (2).
limitations: Static deposited model only; not a measured melting temperature or a claim about the specific energetic contribution of each hydrogen bond.
Base-stacking interactions also contribute substantially to real DNA duplex stability; this question addresses only the hydrogen-bonding count/geometry, not the full thermodynamic picture.
items.answer_text: N1(G)-N3(C) = 2.827 angstrom; N2(G)-O2(C) = 2.817 angstrom; O6(G)-N4(C) = 2.709 angstrom. All three fall in the typical hydrogen-bond distance range (about 2.7-2.9 angstrom), consistent with a genuine Watson-Crick G-C pair. G-C base pairs are expected to be more thermally stable than A-T base pairs at the same position, because a G-C pair forms three hydrogen bonds versus an A-T pair's two: more hydrogen bonds means more favorable interactions must be broken to separate the two strands there, which is part of why GC-rich DNA regions generally have higher melting temperatures than AT-rich regions (base stacking also contributes and is not addressed by this hydrogen-bond count alone).

records.geometric_relation: The standard Watson-Crick G-C base pair forms three hydrogen bonds: guanine N1 to cytosine N3, guanine N2 to cytosine O2, and guanine O6 to cytosine N4. All three donor/acceptor distances are direct measurements on the deposited coordinates for this specific base pair.
records.scientific_result: This entry's own SEQRES record confirms residue 2 of chain A is DG (guanine) and, following the established antiparallel pairing rule (chain A residue i with chain B residue 25-i, already used for BNP003/BNI002), chain B residue 23 is DC (cytosine); the three measured donor/acceptor distances (all in the classic ~2.7-2.9 angstrom hydrogen-bond range) are new evidence confirming a real Watson-Crick geometry at this specific base pair, not assumed from the base identities alone.
conditions: First model, ATOM records only; ideal Watson-Crick atom naming per the deposited residue (N1/N2/O6 for guanine, N3/O2/N4 for cytosine).

All 6 atoms belong to a single base pair; their maximum pairwise separation is under 1 nm, confirmed by direct calculation (unlike combining this pair with a second, spatially distant base pair, whose combined atom set would exceed 1 nm).
limitations: Static deposited crystal model; not a claim about hydrogen-bond dynamics, base-pair breathing, or solution behavior.

items.rubric: 8 points: three distances (6; 0.01 angstrom each), correct identification that G-C pairs (3 hydrogen bonds) are expected to be more thermally stable than A-T pairs (2 hydrogen bonds), with the reasoning that more hydrogen bonds per base pair means more energy is required to separate the strands at that position (2).
limitations: Static deposited model only; not a measured melting temperature or a claim about the specific energetic contribution of each hydrogen bond.
Base-stacking interactions also contribute substantially to real DNA duplex stability; this question addresses only the hydrogen-bonding count/geometry, not the full thermodynamic picture.
items.reference_answer: N1(G)-N3(C) = 2.827 angstrom; N2(G)-O2(C) = 2.817 angstrom; O6(G)-N4(C) = 2.709 angstrom. All three fall in the typical hydrogen-bond distance range (about 2.7-2.9 angstrom), consistent with a genuine Watson-Crick G-C pair. G-C base pairs are expected to be more thermally stable than A-T base pairs at the same position, because a G-C pair forms three hydrogen bonds versus an A-T pair's two: more hydrogen bonds means more favorable interactions must be broken to separate the two strands there, which is part of why GC-rich DNA regions generally have higher melting temperatures than AT-rich regions (base stacking also contributes and is not addressed by this hydrogen-bond count alone).

exclusions: No design task; no melting-temperature measurement claim.
